dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: All 20 person_evidence entries were created with factually correct data. The confidence level of 'confident' is appropriate given the strong correlation across two independent censuses (1860 and 1880) with matching names, ages, and household structure, combined with the documented LDS emigration corridor from Liverpool that explains the England-to-Utah move. The move_bridge field correctly cites the wiki page content about Latter-day Saint emigration. All match_scores (0.78) are supported by same_person tool calls. The tree facts were enriched with residence entries for 1860 and 1880 with proper source references. No fabricated material or unsupported claims.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All 18 assertions from the two census records were linked to appropriate tree persons. The 1860 census (9 assertions) linked to I1, I2, I3, I4 with all name, birth, and residence facts covered. The 1880 census (9 assertions) linked to I1, I2, I4 with name, birth, residence, and relationship assertions (wife and son) linked to both parties as required. Sarah (I3) was correctly noted as absent from 1880 with a plausible explanation. No assertions were omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed arguments matching expected values. same_person calls correctly used assertionId and treePersonId for each assertion-person pair. place_search calls for Salt Lake County and Cranfield matched expected place names. place_distance correctly compared Utah and England locations. wiki_read correctly targeted the Utah_Emigration_and_Immigration page. materialize_facts calls properly specified personId, recordId, and recordRole for each person-record combination. No fixture_not_found errors occurred. Arguments were semantically correct throughout.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: The 'confident' rating is correctly calibrated. The link is supported by two independent census records (1860 and 1880) with strong correlation on name, age, birthplace, and household composition. The move from England to Utah is explained by the documented LDS emigration corridor from Liverpool cited in the wiki page, which directly addresses the geographic gap. The rationale correctly names this corridor as the bridge. The rule does not over-fire here: the corridor is documented on the destination's wiki page and explains the move, so 'confident' is appropriate rather than 'probable'. Chronological consistency is maintained (birth ~1822 matches across records).

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: exact name matches ('Joseph Pratt', 'Ann Pratt', 'Sarah Pratt'), consistent birth years (~1822, ~1825, ~1847, ~1850), England birthplace, household position (head, wife, children), and the documented LDS emigration corridor. The rationales address the geographic move by naming the corridor and distance (7767 km). For relationship assertions, the rationales explain how the assertion bears on each party. The rationales go beyond generic 'names match' statements and provide substantive correlation analysis.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census were correctly linked to both parties. The 'Wife of Joseph Pratt' assertion (a_017) generated two person_evidence entries: one for I2 (the wife) and one for I1 (the named husband). The 'Son of Joseph Pratt' assertion (a_018) generated two entries: one for I4 (the son) and one for I1 (the named father). All relationship-implying assertions have both-side links as required.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons needed to be minted; all four household members (I1, I2, I3, I4) already existed in the tree. The materialize_facts tool was correctly invoked to enrich existing persons with sourced facts from both census records. The 1860 census enriched all four persons with residence facts; the 1880 census enriched I1, I2, and I4. No edges needed to be written because the parent-child and couple relationships already existed in the tree (R1-R5). The skill correctly recognized this and did not create duplicate edges. All facts written carry proper source references (S10 for 1860, S11 for 1880).

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion-person pair where a tree candidate existed. The tool was invoked 12 times across the two censuses, scoring each link at 0.78. The scores were recorded in match_score fields and informed the confidence calibration without overriding it. The score of 0.78 is reasonable for a strong name and age match but not perfect (accounting for the geographic move requiring external validation). The scores did not dictate the 'confident' rating; rather, the documented corridor and multi-source corroboration justified it. For relationship assertions, same_person was called with the appropriate recordRole (head for the husband in a_017 and a_018) to score the right party.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.
